entry.title: docs: ADR-0014, sourced material carries its licence (#66)
entry.content:
docs: ADR-0014, sourced material carries its licence (#66)

Three readers are about to be built for openly licensed material --
Wiktionary via kaikki.org, Lingua Libre recordings, and OpenSubtitles
frequency lists. This is the decision they all reference.

The rule that matters is not the parsing. courses/ is CC BY-SA 4.0 and
emit.py writes a course directory, so a reader that hands back a bare
string has dropped the only thing that decides whether it may be used.
Every item therefore carries its provenance, and the licence is recorded
per item -- a Lingua Libre recording is CC BY-SA 4.0 or CC0 depending on
the recording.

Three licence states rather than two, using SPDX's own tokens. kaikki
states "the same licenses as Wiktionary - both CC-BY-SA and GFDL" with no
version numbers, so a two-state model has to either invent a version or
throw away the fact that terms exist. LicenseRef- is the third state and
it costs nothing.

The property is redistributable, not exportable: a floor, not a permit.
CC BY-NC-SA is perfectly well known and unshippable, and this repository
already documents that exact case in THIRD-PARTY.md.

Also settles two questions the work would otherwise have decided in code:
these packages are stdlib-only and add no extra, because nothing in them
needs a third-party package; and wordfreq stays as it is, because it
answers whether a distractor is about as common as the answer, not what
word number 500 is.

Numbered 0014 because 0013 is taken on another branch.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: docs: a page about exercise types, with examples that run
entry.content:
docs: a page about exercise types, with examples that run

Generated from the registry by `scripts/gen_types_doc.py`, with a CI check that
it is current -- the same argument as the schema page: a hand-written list of six
types and their fields would be wrong within a month and believed anyway.

The examples are not screenshots. The script copies the app's own renderers into
`docs/javascripts/repetita/` and the page renders each type with them, so a
picture of an exercise cannot drift from the exercise. The word bank assembles,
the multiple choice selects, and a line under each one says nothing is graded,
because there is no server behind a static site and answering does nothing.

Two quoting bugs found by looking rather than reasoning: the payload travels in
an HTML attribute, so it is escaped now (an apostrophe in any future example
would have ended the attribute early), and the `picture` placeholder is base64
rather than a literal SVG full of quotes.

That placeholder is drawn rather than photographed on purpose. Neither course has
`picture` material, so there is no licensed image to show, and hotlinking one
would have put an unattributed image in the documentation of a project whose
rule about images is the strictest it has.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(content): an exercise type is a file, and a course can declare one
entry.content:
feat(content): an exercise type is a file, and a course can declare one

CONTRIBUTING promises that 'a new scheduler, grader, presenter or session policy
is a new file plus a registry entry'. The exercise type was the one extension
point that was not like that: six of them in a single hard-coded dict, so adding
one meant editing the engine -- which is why the Create tab shipped with a type
picker over a fixed list and no way to want another.

Now: `content/notetypes/` is a package with one declaration per file and a
registry in the same shape as `graders/` and `srs/`, and a course may declare
its own in `notetypes.yaml`, merged over the built-ins.

**And declarations are checked, which they never were.** Nothing verified that a
template's grader existed -- a typo was a LookupError at answer time, on a card
in front of a learner. Once a course can write one, that stops being
unreachable, so a declaration is now refused by name when it points at a field
the type does not have, an unknown grader, a form that grader cannot judge, or
no cards at all. A broken type is dropped and reported rather than merged: its
notes would otherwise be quarantined for a reason that is not their fault.

Running those checks against the built-in six found two real ones, both
declaring a form their grader cannot mark and both unreachable behind an earlier
form, so nobody had ever met them: `phrase.say` offered a word bank to the
`self` grader (issue #57) and `vocab.recognize` a flashcard to `typed`. Fixed.

It also found a check of mine that was wrong. 'The expect field must not be
shown before' sounds right and would forbid the most common exercise shape there
is: in `vocab`, `l1` is the prompt for `produce` and the answer for
`recognize`. `NoteType.visible_before` already excludes a card's own answer
unconditionally, so the field-level setting is a default and the card wins. The
check is gone and the reasoning is in its place.

On the client, `static/types/` is the same idea: one view per type, registered,
with the generic renderer as the fallback for a type that has no file. A gap now
marks its blank inside the sentence and shows its cue as the grammatical label it
is; a transform shows its instruction as a task rather than a second sentence.
The four `modes/` files each changed by one import line.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: docs: the rules become mechanisms
entry.content:
docs: the rules become mechanisms

About seventy rules across nine documents, and the shape of nearly all of them
was prohibition: 'never' appears eleven times in this file alone, and 'never
change an existing item id' was repeated in twelve places.

Every one had a real reason -- the id rule protects the only thing here that
cannot be reconstructed. But a prohibition has no idea what it costs, and three
costs were being paid daily: an id derived from a typo stayed wrong for ever,
rubbish could only be archived and never removed, and small fixes became issues
that nobody did.

So a prohibition is replaced by a mechanism wherever one can exist. Four rules
remain absolute, and they are the ones no mechanism helps with: history is never
destroyed silently, answers do not reach an open question, the scheduler is
pure, the engine knows no language. Licensing is separate -- not a rule about
care but the condition for the repository existing.

The id rule is stronger than it was, not weaker. It used to rely on everybody
reading it in twelve places; now the only way to do it moves the history, CI
checks the record, and a record pointing at nothing is refused.

Three things still ask first, about consequence rather than permission: deleting
study history, deleting material still in a course, and human-only issues.
Pushing and publishing are not among them -- and `enforce_admins` is off, with
the four required checks kept, so this commit goes straight to main.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(store): rename an id with its history, and delete material on pu…
entry.content:
feat(store): rename an id with its history, and delete material on purpose (#65)

* feat(store): rename an id with its history, and delete material on purpose

Two prohibitions become two operations.

**`repetita rename-id <old> <new>`.** Ids were frozen because a rename orphans
history: scheduling state is keyed on the card id, which is keyed on the note id.
That is true of renaming by hand, and says nothing about whether the operation is
possible. It is -- it just has to happen in one transaction across everything
that refers to the exercise, which is nine tables and ten columns, which is
exactly why it belongs in a function rather than in a rule telling people not to.

It refuses a target that is already taken, **including by an archived note**: an
archived exercise still owns the history stored under its id. And it clears
`origin`, which is what stops the next import from archiving the exercise that
was just renamed -- the file still says the old id until an export catches up,
so until then the note is one that was never in a file. A test caught that; it
is the fourth time this rule has been needed.

**`repetita purge`.** Archiving stays the default and stays right. What was
missing was any way to be rid of a test set or a duplicated import. It reports
before it acts -- how many exercises, how many cards, how much history is
attached -- does nothing without `--yes`, and refuses `--with-history` without
`--i-mean-it`, because those rows cannot be rebuilt from anything. A snapshot is
taken first either way.

**And CI learns the difference.** A proper rename looks identical to an id
vanishing, which is the thing `check-ids` exists to catch, so the rename is
written down in `courses/<course>/renames.yaml` and the check reads it -- but
only accepts a record whose new id is actually there. The rule stops being
"never rename", which nothing could enforce and which left wrong ids wrong for
ever, and becomes "a rename is written down", which CI can check and a reviewer
can read.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* style: sort the imports in the restore command

entry.title: feat(store): snapshots of the study database, taken correctly (#64)
entry.content:
feat(store): snapshots of the study database, taken correctly (#64)

`card_state` and `review_log` are the only things here that cannot be rebuilt
from anything: material comes back from `courses/`, a schedule does not. That is
why so much of this package is written as a prohibition. A snapshot is what makes
the carefulness affordable -- with one in hand a mistake is a restore, and an
operation that would otherwise have to be forbidden can simply be offered.

`repetita snapshot ["why"]` · `--list` · `repetita restore <name>`, and
`restore` snapshots what it is about to overwrite, because restoring is itself
the destructive step and the state it replaces is usually the one nobody thought
worth keeping until a second later.

**Through SQLite's backup API, not `cp`.** In WAL mode committed rows live in
the log until a checkpoint folds them into the main file, so a file copy is
complete only if it happens to be taken after one: a race, whose losing side is a
backup that opens cleanly and is quietly missing the last answers.

Checked rather than asserted, and my first version of this message was wrong:
the seven hand-made copies already in `data/` all open and all look sane. They
won the race. The test provokes the losing side deterministically -- an open
connection and fifty committed rows -- because a backup that is correct by luck
is the kind that fails on the day it is needed.

`scripts/restart-host.sh` stops rolling its own `cp` and calls this; automatic
snapshots are named so that pruning keeps the last twenty and never touches one
somebody took deliberately.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: fix(create): let go of unsaved work, on purpose (#63)
entry.content:
fix(create): let go of unsaved work, on purpose (#63)

Leaving the Create tab kept everything in memory and said nothing, which is kind
right up until the day you want the half-typed rows gone -- and then there was
nowhere to say so. The only discard in the tab appeared while switching sets.

Two ways out now, both through the same bar: a **Discard changes** button beside
Save, and the guard firing when you click another tab, offering Save them first
/ Discard them / Stay here. Leaving with nothing unsaved is instant, as before.

Discarding actually puts the rows back before it navigates. Leaving them in
memory meant the guard stopped you again on the way out, over work you had just
said you did not want.

The router grew a hook for this rather than Create reaching into the tab
buttons: a view may refuse to be left, and answers by calling `show` again
itself once the question is settled.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(ui): show what is waiting, and say what just happened (#62)
entry.content:
feat(ui): show what is waiting, and say what just happened (#62)

Two things were invisible, and both read as the app ignoring you.

**Everything you told the app disappeared.** Changes staged on Manage could only
be seen on Manage; lesson notes only inside the composer that makes them; cards
flagged while studying and problems filed from Design **nowhere at all** --
`open_reports()` and `open_issues()` existed and no screen called either. The
first thing the new panel did on the real database was surface a card flagged as
"bad translation" that had been sitting unseen since it was reported.

`GET /api/waiting` is assembly only -- `material.diff`, `drafts.queued`,
`reports.open_reports`, `issues.open_issues` -- and a header count that is on
every tab, so a staged change is no longer invisible the moment you look away.

**Every confirmation rendered about 2,200px below the fold.** `#status` is one
grey span in the page footer; on a wrapped board that is off screen, it was never
cleared, and it has no live region. Saves, warnings and failures all landed
there. They are toasts now, in the corner of the window, with failures that stay
until dismissed.

Three silences get a voice: Confirm had **no `catch` at all**, so a failed
confirm showed nothing whatever; Design's "Something's off here" said nothing on
success and threw an unhandled rejection on failure; and staging a change now
updates the drawer **in place** rather than rebuilding the panel, because that
swapped the Confirm button between mousedown and mouseup -- pressing Confirm
straight from a field you had just edited did nothing at all.

And the inbox is called **Capture a lesson**. "Add material" is what a person
presses when they want to add material, and it was the one route that does not:
it queues text for an agent to shape later. The direct way is the Create tab, and
the label should not compete with it.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(ui): Create writes, Manage files (#61)
entry.content:
feat(ui): Create writes, Manage files (#61)

Both tabs edited exercises, with two editors, two field orders and two different
promises about when a change lands. That is most of why adding and editing
material felt like a maze: before you could act you had to decide which tab you
were in, and the app never said.

**Manage's inspector becomes a filing card.** The fields are there to be read --
in reading order, not the alphabetical order a JSON object arrives in, which put
`audio` first and the actual question fourth -- each still labelled shown with
the question or shown after answering, which is the best explanation of an
exercise in the app. It is titled by the exercise's **name** rather than
`fala-capoeiristas.01`, a directory and a sequence number.

What stays editable there is what filing means: the name, the tags, and **which
set it is in** -- a control, because dragging was the only way to move an
exercise, which is fine when two sets are side by side and impossible when they
are four rows apart.

**"Edit this exercise →" opens Create on that exercise**, not merely on its set.
Losing your place was most of the friction in moving between the two.

**Create owns naming a set, properly.** Choosing a set and naming one were the
same control and one trap: picking an existing set and typing in the id box
renamed nothing -- it quietly pointed Save at a different set, so the next edit
moved that one exercise into a set that did not exist and left the other
twenty-four behind. Renaming is now its own act, through the endpoint that moves
every note in one transaction, and it was never called by any UI until now.

Three more dead ends in Create, each of which read as the app ignoring you:

* editing **tags** alone left Save greyed out for ever, because the listener
  refreshed nothing;
* naming a **new set** and pressing Save did nothing, so the only way to make one
  was a button on another tab that created nothing either;
* **switching sets discarded everything typed since the last Save**, silently.
  Now you are asked, and closing the tab with unsaved work says so too -- there
  was no `beforeunload` anywhere in the app.

And changing an exercise's **type** no longer deletes the fields the new type
does not have. They are set aside and come back if the type does.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: fix(manage): say where a drop will land (#60)
entry.content:
fix(manage): say where a drop will land (#60)

Dragging answered "where will this go?" with a border around the column under
the pointer, which says *which* column and not *where* -- and the answer was
always "before this one", which is not what an outlined box means to anybody.
Reported as: you cannot tell where the set will land.

A set now shows a **caret in the gap it will drop into**, and which gap depends
on which half of the column the pointer is in. That also fixes something that
was not possible before: `moveUnit` only ever inserted *before* the target, so
no set could be moved to the end of the board. Dropping on the right of the last
column now does it.

An exercise marks the set that will **receive** it -- it marked nothing at all
before, because the highlight was only applied to set-drags. Deliberately a
tinted column rather than a caret: dropping an exercise *into* a set and dropping
a set *between* sets are different acts, and two gestures that look alike are two
gestures you have to guess between.

Also: the column you are holding is dimmed and dashed, so you can see what you
picked up; `dragend` clears the marks, which is the handler that was missing
when a drag abandoned over nothing left its last highlight on the board; the set
handle is a visible grip and the remove button is no longer `opacity: 0` until
hovered -- at zero it was not quiet, it was undiscoverable; and the Confirm
drawer is sticky, so the button you have to press is not six rows of board above
where you are working.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat: a Create tab — exercises can be written in the app (#59)
entry.content:
feat: a Create tab — exercises can be written in the app (#59)

* feat(store): write material, not only edit it

`save_set` is the first path in this package that creates a note rather than
editing what an import left. Two columns carry that and both are load-bearing:
`origin` stays empty, which is what tells an import the note was never in a
file, and `edited_at` is set, which keeps its cards from being recomputed from
a file that does not mention it.

The first of those closes a hole that would have destroyed the feature on the
next restart: `sync()` archived every note it could not find in the files, with
no exemption for one the app had written. Fourth appearance of one rule --
notes, cards, units, and now notes again for the ones that begin life here.

Also: `notes.forms` (migration 7), a per-card form preference for exercises
whose author disagreed with their type, applied in `expand_cards` so that both
paths into the cards table get it from one place; `GRADER_FORMS`, because a
flashcard cannot be marked by anything but the `self` grader and nothing about
the result would look wrong from the outside; and `ids.propose`, which derives
an id from the answer and checks it against every id the database has ever
held, archived ones included.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* feat(web): endpoints for writing exercises, and a dry run for the screen

`POST /api/sets/<set>/exercises` saves a whole set -- new exercises, edits to
ones already there, removals -- in one request and applies it. Writing an
exercise is not editing one: there is no older version to be careful of, so the
Save button is the confirmation rather than a trip to the Manage drawer.

`POST /api/material/check` is the same shape of payload with nothing written,
answering what the authoring screen needs while you type: the name this exercise
would get, the cards it would make, its leaks and warnings, and which forms it
could be asked in **with the reason for each one it could not**. A route rather
than a rule reimplemented in the browser, because the leak test is
accent-sensitive and word-boundary aware and a second copy of it would
eventually disagree with the one that decides what gets served.

`/api/material` now sends each note type's cards as well as its fields, with
`visible_before` composed by `NoteType.visible_before` on this side -- it is not
a list of fields marked 'before', and recomposing it client-side is how a field
ends up shown in one view and hidden in another.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* feat(web): a Create tab, where exercises are written

A set down the left, the exercise you are on in the middle, and on the right
what it will look like to a learner -- rendered by the same module the Study tab
uses, so the preview is the exercise rather than a picture of one. Paste a list
of lines to make several at once; pick any of the six types; choose how each one
is asked, with the reason shown for every form that is not available rather than
the form quietly disappearing.

Nothing in create.js decides validity. Whether a field gives away its answer,
what an exercise will be called, which forms it can be asked in -- all of it
comes back from /api/material/check as you type, because a second opinion in
JavaScript would eventually disagree with the one that decides what is served.

The tab router was four booleans and eight toggle lines for three views, and a
fourth by the same method is how it gets to six; it is now one row per view.

Two bugs found by building on top of it:

* `_reexpand` wrote only the cards that were missing, so the `ON CONFLICT`
  clause that brings an existing card back in line with its note never ran --
  choosing a different form for an exercise that already existed changed the
  note and left the card asking the old way.
* Distractors were built from the *files* rather than from the database, so an
  exercise written in the app contributed none and received none, and could
  never be offered as a multiple choice however many wrong answers were typed
  into it. They are now derived from the material as the database has it, which
  is what ADR-0006 made the material.

Manage's '+ New set' hands over here instead of asking for a name in a prompt
box, and its inspector gains a link to the set in Create. One place to write.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* docs: writing exercises in the app

ADR-0010 records the decision and the two things that had to be true for it: the
`origin` rule -- the fourth appearance of 'whatever the app creates must record
that it did, or the next import undoes it' -- and distractors being derived from
the database rather than from the files. It also records the per-exercise form
preference as a real departure from ADR-0001, where presentation belonged to the
card and to the moment.

The four ways in are five, and the in-app route is no longer 'fix one exercise'.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* refactor(core): the grader-form rule belongs to the domain, not the web layer

`store/` may not import `web/`, and it was doing so to find out which forms a
grader can mark -- a fact about grading rather than about drawing, so it moves to
`core/forms.py` along with the vocabulary of form names. `SUPPORTED_FORMS` stays
in `serialize.py`, where it means something different: what this build can put on
a screen.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* fix(create): save only what changed, and refuse what cannot be stored

Opening a set and pressing Save rewrote every exercise in it, which is not
nothing: a rewritten note is marked edited-here, and from then on a change to it
in the course files is a conflict rather than an update. Save now sends the rows
that are new, changed or on their way out, and the footer counts the same ones --
'10 changed' on a set nobody had touched was the visible half of it.

Also in the write path: a field is coerced to the type its note type declares, so
a list that arrives as one string is not stored as a string and read back as a
list on the next import; and a malformed lesson date is refused rather than
dropped, because a dropped one pushes a whole set to the back of the
introduction order, which looks exactly like the app ignoring today's lesson.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: fix(manage): hold the scroll position, and let the board be rearrange…
entry.content:
fix(manage): hold the scroll position, and let the board be rearranged (#56)

Three things about the board, all reported from using it.

**Expanding a word moved the view.** Every interaction here redraws by
replacing nodes, and a replaced scroll container starts again at the top-left --
so opening a word six sets along threw the board back to the first column and
the column back to its first row. `render()` and `renderBoard()` now record
where the reader was (the page, and each column's own scroll) and put it back
afterwards. In `render()` rather than at the one call site, because staging an
edit, selecting and saving a name all go through the same path.

**Thirty sets no longer run off to the right.** `.mboard` wraps, so columns flow
into as many rows as the width allows and the board is scrolled like a page --
six rows of five at 1600px instead of one strip six screens long. Columns are
shorter to suit (`min(60vh, 30rem)`), and the phone keeps `nowrap` with its
scroll-snap: wrapping is the answer to "they are too far apart", and on a phone
nothing is beside anything anyway.

**A column can be dragged by its header.** The reason the distance mattered was
dragging exercises between two distant sets; now the sets can be put side by
side first. `dragging` was a bare array of note ids, which cannot say what is
being dragged, so it is tagged -- `{kind: "notes", ids}` or `{kind: "unit", id}`
-- and a column's existing drop handler branches on it.

The arrangement is a property of this screen and nothing else: it lives in
`localStorage`, reconciled with the live set list on load so a remembered layout
can never decide which sets exist, and **it never reaches the server**.
`units.ord` is untouched, nothing is staged, and the exported course is
byte-identical before and after. A **Reset layout** button appears in the
toolbar only while the board is actually arranged differently from the course.

Verified in a browser against a copy of the live database: expanding a word at
scroll 1200 leaves it at 1200; a column's own scrollTop of 220 survives a
redraw; dragging the last set onto the first reorders it, the order survives a
reload, Reset restores the course order and clears the key; `/api/material/pending`
is empty throughout. At 500px the board still snaps one set at a time and the
page does not scroll sideways.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat: every exercise has a name, an inbox for raw material, removable…
entry.content:
feat: every exercise has a name, an inbox for raw material, removable sets (#55)

* feat: every exercise has a name, an inbox for raw material, removable sets

Three screens needed to refer to one exercise in a few characters -- the board,
the confirm drawer, the plan preview -- and all three fell back to the note id.
`gram-atras-passado-ainda.tempo-01` is a directory name and a sequence number.

**Names.** `notes.label` + `notes.label_custom`, migration 6, derived by
`content/labels.py` and editable in the inspector. The rule was chosen by
measurement over the 757 live notes, and the obvious ordering lost: reaching for
the cue head first -- which looks right, it is already the family key -- gives a
median of 10 characters, a longest of 72 and 39% repeating within a set, against
the answer's 6, 20 and 20%. A family key is *designed* to be shared.

Names repeat, and that is not a bug to fix: twenty exercises in one set
legitimately answer `o`. The board shows what separates two rows with the same
name (`03`, `07`, `cinema`) and only there, rather than inventing text nobody
wrote. A typed name is pinned and exported; a derived one is neither.

**The inbox.** `material_drafts`, `store/drafts.py`, `repetita inbox`, and the
"Add material" button that replaces "Import from the course files". Raw text,
stored unparsed on purpose -- a lesson is written down in one state of mind and
turned into exercises in another, and making the first wait for the second loses
the note. ADR-0009.

**Removable sets.** A `remove_set` change kind staged like every other, so the
drawer says how much goes with it before you agree. Archived, never deleted.

Three fixes fell out of building it:

* An import un-archived a set removed here: `archived_at=NULL` was
  unconditional, and the directory is still in `courses/`. Third time this rule
  has been needed -- notes, then cards, now units.
* `_preview_names` samples before the query. `budget` comes from the request,
  and one placeholder per card meets SQLite's limit of 999 as a 500.
* Confirm reported "0 notes updated" after removing an empty set. True, and not
  what happened.

The Import button is removed rather than deprecated, with #54 asking whether the
capability is wanted at all; the `/api/import/*` endpoints are untouched and
startup still imports.

**The documentation site.** `mkdocs.yml`, built to Pages by a new workflow --
the `docs` extra has been declared in pyproject since the beginning and never
switched on. Two audiences: how to study, design and manage, and the four ways
to add material (with who does the work in each); then how it works, with
mermaid diagrams of the three data lifecycles, note->card->form, and what an
import decides. `docs/schema.md` is generated from the `SCHEMA` string by
`scripts/gen_schema_doc.py`, with a CI check that it has not drifted -- the
comments in the schema are the documentation, and a hand-copied page would lose
them and then be believed anyway.

Pages needs switching on under Settings -> Pages -> Source: GitHub Actions.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* ci: let the Pages deploy fail until Pages is enabled

The build is the part that can break and stays required; the deploy step has
nowhere to publish to until Settings -> Pages -> Source is GitHub Actions, and a
setting nobody has changed yet should not paint main red.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat: a design pass over Study, Design and Manage (#53)
entry.content:
feat: a design pass over Study, Design and Manage (#53)

* feat(store): one definition of how well material is known

Groundwork for the design pass: three screens are about to ask "how well do I
know this?", and answering it three times would produce three numbers that
disagree about the same cards.

The obvious metric does not survive contact with the data. Measured on the real
database -- 757 live cards -- the buckets are 673 new, 31 retired, 25 young, 24
learning, 4 suspended, and **0 mature**. Nothing has reached the 21-day
threshold, so "how much of this set is mature" paints every set the same grey
today and keeps doing so for three weeks.

The second trap is "I know this". All 31 retired cards are `declared` -- a claim
the learner made, not evidence the scheduler gathered. Excluding them makes a
set marked entirely known read as nothing known; folding them into `mature`
promotes the claim to evidence, which is the one distinction `declare_known`
exists to preserve. So `core/mastery.py` keeps four states and reports the claim
separately, and the interface can render it as a claim.

Deliberately not accuracy from `review_log`: per-set accuracy is dominated by
leeches -- one card answered eleven times at 9% drags a whole set -- so it would
measure what annoyed someone rather than what they know.

Families come from the cue, not the id. The id stem is the obvious key and was
measured and rejected: 404 groups for 676 notes, 350 singletons, and its biggest
"families" were a topic plus a sequence number. What is actually authored is
`cue: "morar — imperfeito, eu"`, on 540 of 560 gap notes, and splitting a string
on a separator is not knowledge of Portuguese. On the real course that yields
292 notes in families with readable variant labels, and zero false families in
`licao-2026-09-06-genero` -- the set the id rule got most wrong.

A set can now be created and renamed here. That needed `units.edited_at`, for
the third time in this stack: an import archives every unit it cannot find in
the files, and a set made in the app is in none of them. Notes have `edited_at`,
cards follow their note, and units had nothing. Renaming a unit is safe in a way
renaming a note id is not -- nothing in `card_state` references a unit -- and
`notes.unit` is updated in the same transaction.

Notes now carry the label the board will show: the question and the answer,
composed from the note type's own `ask`/`expect` so a row is labelled with the
fields the study path asks it with. The field the family already names is
dropped from the row, or a `gap` note would print its cue twice.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* feat(web): a design pass over Study, Design and Manage

The engine was well reasoned and the interface was a placeholder. One 640px cap
served three very different jobs, raw keys leaked into the page, and hierarchy
was font-size and nothing else.

**Width follows the job.** The shell is told which tab it is showing. Study
stays narrow because a long line of Portuguese is harder to read, not easier;
Design gets two panes; Manage gets the monitor. That single cap was why a board
of 27 sets rendered as two ragged columns.

**One encoding for "how well do I know this", used by all three.** A dot for the
glance, a bar for the composition, and the claim kept visibly apart from the
evidence -- "I know this" is hatched, never solid, because a solid block would
say a claim and a learned card are the same thing.

**Study** gets the session as a shape rather than a countdown. `33 left` pinned
at the batch size while the per-card number kept moving; a row of marks is one
idea instead of two that disagree. Field names are gone from the card: a learner
reading "cue: morar — imperfeito, eu" was being shown the database's word for a
hint. The role is carried by how it looks instead.

**Design** replaces an "Add a topic…" dropdown with every topic visible, with
its size and how far into it you are. A dropdown asks you to remember what
exists. Priority rows show the share the curve actually gives them, so "top of
the list" has a number attached, and the knobs read as sentences that update
rather than `template_bias` on a slider from 0 to 3.

"Practise this plan" is refused when the plan is empty. With no priorities the
policy has no mix to honour and falls back to serving whatever comes next --
which is the Study tab, reached by a button claiming to be something else.

**Manage** shows the exercise instead of a truncated id, with the answer beside
it, families collapsed, and a search box. Columns are fixed-width and scroll
independently; sets run from 5 to 76 exercises and one shared scroll let the
tallest decide where everything else sat.

Three bugs found by looking at it rather than by testing it:

* Every `<script type="module">` is its own job and microtasks drain between
  them, so routing queued with `queueMicrotask` ran before `manage.js` had
  registered its listener -- the Manage tab opened blank when linked to and
  worked when clicked.
* `node.append(x)` stringifies anything that is not a Node, so a conditional
  child written as `cond ? el(…) : null` printed the literal word "null" on the
  page. `fill()` filters, as `el()` already did.
* A flex item will not shrink below its content unless told to, and the rows are
  `nowrap`, so a 22rem column rendered at 1000px.

Tabs are linkable, which is how the screenshots above were taken at all.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat: the Manage tab — edit the material the database owns (#52)
entry.content:
feat: the Manage tab — edit the material the database owns (#52)

* chore(scripts): restart the app serving repetita, with a backup first

Picking up a code change means restarting whatever is serving repetita, and the
host serves it live from this working tree. By hand that is three commands, one
of which is `kill`, and the one worth never forgetting is the backup -- a restart
picks up new code, and new code may migrate the study database.

It reads the command line and working directory off the running process and
starts it again the same way, so it does not need to know whether repetita is
running standalone or mounted inside a host application.

Keyed on the port. Holding the study database open would have been a nicer
signal -- no configuration at all -- but repetita opens the database per request
and closes it at teardown, so between requests nobody holds it. The port is
remembered in a gitignored file after the first run: which port someone runs
their own host on is not a property of the project.

SIGTERM first, SIGKILL only if it is ignored: a server mid-write deserves the
chance to close the database cleanly. Schema version and history counts are
printed before and after, so a migration is visible rather than something you
discover later.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* feat(web): study from the design tab, and let a plan order the practice

Two things the designer was missing.

**Studying from it.** A plan was something you could build and preview and then
had to go elsewhere to use. "Study with this plan" activates it and asks the
session loop for a fresh queue -- through `/api/session` like everything else,
because a plan is not a separate mode. It is the order the ordinary daily queue
is built in.

**Ordering the practice, not only the mix.** The priority list decided which
*new* material was introduced; the owed cards still arrived in due-date order
regardless, so a learner who said numbers matter most met numbers after forty
cards of something else. Now the debt is ordered by the plan too.

What that must never mean is a smaller debt. Every owed card is still in the
list and still served in the same session -- the plan decides what you meet
first, not what you get out of. A learner who could hide two hundred owed cards
behind a priority list would, once, and find them again a month later at four
times the size. There is a test for it rather than a comment.

Python's sort is stable, so most-overdue-first is not discarded; it becomes the
tie-break within each priority.

The tab now says all of this in a sentence, with the real owed count in it. The
alternative reading -- that a plan is a filter, and picking one lets you study
only what you feel like -- is the one that would quietly bury a backlog, so it
is worth closing off in the interface and not only in the code.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* feat(web): a plan is an additional path, practised from the design tab

The previous commit had an active plan take over the daily queue. That was
wrong, for a plain reason: a learner who builds a plan, tries it and dislikes it
should get their ordinary session back by clicking away from it -- not by
deleting the plan.

So the Study tab is the course's own order and nothing alters it. A session is
built under a plan only when the request names one, and the designer has its own
practice view where that happens. "Leave the plan" is one click.

Which plan a request is studying under is now a property of the request rather
than a global "active plan". The two paths are two ways through one set of
material, and which one you are on is what you asked for, not a mode the
application is in.

An answer records a revision only when it was given under a plan. An answer from
the Study tab is not evidence about any plan, and filing it under whichever
happened to be active would make every later comparison wrong -- the exact
failure `plan_revision_id` exists to prevent, arriving by a different door.

The client says which plan it was practising; the server resolves which revision
that is. Same reason `form` is recomputed on the way in: the log is a record of
what happened, and a client is free to lie.

A bar above the session names the plan while one is in force, so what is on
screen is never ambiguous about which path produced it.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* fix(web): make `hidden` actually hide

Leaving a plan hid nothing: the bar stayed on screen, still offering to leave a
plan that had already been left.

`hidden` carries `display: none` only from the user-agent stylesheet, so any
author rule that sets `display` on the same element beats it. `.plan-bar` is
`display: flex`, which is the ordinary shape for a toggled row and therefore
exactly the case that breaks. `.stage` and `.designer` set no display at all,
which is the only reason they were unaffected.

Fixed once with a `[hidden]` rule rather than a `.plan-bar[hidden]` override,
because the next person to add a hideable flex row will not know they need one.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* feat(web): practising a plan serves the plan's material

The designer said "26 owed cards come first either way", and that was the wrong
promise to make. It was right when a plan *replaced* daily study -- letting a
priority list defer the debt would have been a way to avoid the only part that
demonstrably works. It stopped being right when practice became a second path:
asking to work on food and directions and being handed twenty-six cards of
something else is not practising what you designed.

So a practice session is scoped to the plan. Owed cards from those topics come
first, because answering something already owed is worth more than meeting
something new. Owed cards from elsewhere are not dragged in, and new material is
not padded out with unrelated cards once the plan's own runs out -- a short
session is the honest answer to a narrow plan.

None of that hides anything. The debt the session did not cover is still owed,
still counted, and still served by the Study tab, which no plan alters. That is
what makes scoping safe here and unsafe in the earlier shape.

`scoped` is a parameter rather than the only behaviour, because a plan shaping a
full session and a plan carving one out are different questions, and the second
should not quietly answer the first.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* fix(policies): the introduction gate does not throttle a practice you asked for

Practising a plan of food and directions served three cards while thirty-eight
sat available. The gate was doing it: closed on recent accuracy, so only
fresh-lesson material got through, and scoping to the plan's topics left almost
nothing.

The gate is a brake on material arriving *unasked*. It opens while recent
answers hold up and closes on evidence of overload, which is exactly right for a
queue the learner did not choose. A scoped practice is the opposite situation --
they named the topics and pressed the button -- and braking there is not a
protection, it is a refusal.

Bounded either way: `batch` still caps the session, the material is still only
what the plan asked for, and anything taken on appears in tomorrow's queue where
the gate does apply. Deciding to work hard on a topic is the learner's call, in
the same way "I know this" is.

The daily path is untouched: no plan, no scope, gate as before.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* feat: the Manage tab -- edit the material the database owns

A third tab for managing the course: sets as columns, exercises dragged between
them, an editor per exercise, tags, and a Confirm that applies everything at
once. Importing from the course files shows what clashes with your edits and
asks before overwriting any of it. ADR-0008 covers the part that is a decision.

## The serving path had to follow ownership first

ADR-0006 made the database the owner of the material, and only half of that was
implemented: `build_library` merged the files in and then served `result.notes`,
the *file* version. So the tab as asked for was impossible -- you would fix a
typo, press Confirm, and study the old text until you had exported to YAML and
reloaded. It was invisible until now only because the one in-app writer was
`store/tags.py`, and tags are not served.

Fixing it moved a safety property. `validate.check` -- which refuses a note that
gives away its own answer -- ran in the loader, over notes fresh out of a file.
Serving from the database means an edit reaches a learner without passing it, so
it now runs over whatever the database holds, however it got there. Without that
this change would have turned the Manage tab into a way to ship an exercise that
teaches nothing while looking entirely normal.

## Editing

Changes are staged server-side and applied in one transaction. Server-side
because a refresh, a second tab or a closed laptop should not lose work, and
because Confirm can then show what will actually change rather than a count.

Every write sets `edited_at` and leaves `content_hash` alone. That pair is what
lets an import tell an edit from a file change: forget the first and the next
import silently overwrites the edit; recompute the second and conflict detection
stops working at all.

Two things are refused. A note `id` cannot change -- it is the key progress is
stored under, and `repetita check-ids` only diffs committed YAML in a pull
request, so it would notice long after the damage. A `notetype` cannot change
either: it decides which cards exist.

Removal is archiving, cards included. An import no longer un-archives a note that
was removed here, because the file still has it and the learner would otherwise
watch material they deleted reappear with no explanation.

## Importing

`preview_import` answers what an import would do without doing any of it, and
shares `merge_decision` with the import itself so the two cannot disagree. A
clash shows both versions; a note you do not choose keeps the version you have.
Defaulting the other way would mean an import destroyed work through omission,
which is the one outcome a confirmation step exists to prevent.

## What the review caught

Seven defects, every one of which passed ruff, mypy and the full suite. They all
live where two correct pieces meet, which is where the tests were not looking:

* `sync()` recomputed the cards of app-edited notes from the file, so an edit's
  effect on the card set was undone by the reload in the same request. Adding
  audio created `#listen` and archived it moments later; archiving a note left
  its cards live and orphaned. Whoever owns the note now owns its cards.
* A null payload was accepted and then wedged the tab permanently -- pending and
  confirm both failed from then on, and Discard lives inside the drawer that
  pending draws.
* `preview()` ignored the `scoped` flag, so the pane whose whole job is to be
  believed padded its numbers with material the session would not serve.
* Non-fatal warnings were reported as leaks, which teaches people to ignore the
  alarm that matters.
* The page applied an edit before the server had accepted it, so a failed stage
  left the new value on screen and lost it at the next load.
* A well-formed but unknown plan id silently served the plain session and filed
  the answers with no revision.
* `preview_import` missed the un-archive an import performs, which is exactly
  the preview/import disagreement it exists to prevent.

Each has the test that would have caught it, and all of them are
integration-shaped for the same reason the bugs were not found: the units were
fine.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat: design my lessons — catalogue, tag curation, study plans and th…
entry.content:
feat: design my lessons — catalogue, tag curation, study plans and the tab (#51)

* feat: design my lessons -- catalogue, tag curation, study plans and the tab

Chunks A, B and C of the plan in one change: the material becomes visible, the
learner's intent becomes data, and the tab puts both in front of them.

ADR-0007 covers the part that is a decision rather than a feature.

## The catalogue

`card_state` gains a denormalised `bucket`, written from the single definition in
`core/buckets.py`. Stored rather than recomputed: a threshold that decides policy
must not get a second definition in a WHERE clause, which is the exact shape of
the bug ADR-0002 records. `sync` backfills any state that has none, because a
column added by a migration starts NULL and COALESCE would then report every card
a learner has ever answered as new -- a catalogue confidently wrong about their
own progress.

`store/catalogue.py` is one query and one selector language.
`level=A2,track=gramatica,topic=preposicoes,state=new` is the same string whether
it arrives from the CLI, the web API, or a row in `plan_priorities`; three
parsers for one idea is how they drift. Repeating a dimension widens rather than
contradicts, because two checkboxes mean "either" and contradiction would make an
empty result look like an empty course.

## Curating tags

`repetita tag add|remove|rename|split|merge|list`, all with `--dry-run`. A rename
is course-wide -- a tag renamed on half the material is two tags, which is the
situation this exists to fix rather than to create -- and leaves a `tag_aliases`
row so plans and facets.yaml keep resolving. Every operation marks the notes it
touched as `edited_at`, which is what stops the next import overwriting the change
and makes a genuine clash surface as a conflict.

`repetita export` is owed from ADR-0006 and lands here. The README promises that
adding a lesson is a pull request a non-programmer can make, and once material is
editable in the app that promise depends entirely on writing it back out. It is
also what makes a tag change reviewable: a normal diff on normal files. Note
emission reuses `importers.emit`, so imported and exported material come out in
one format rather than two that drift.

## Plans

Four tables, and `review_log.plan_revision_id`. That column is the reason this is
an ADR: ADR-0003 exists because the predecessor kept aggregates and threw the
sequence away, and "did making it harder actually help?" is the same shape of
question. Adding the link later would work from that day forward and leave every
earlier answer unattributable.

Weights read a priority list as a Zipf curve rather than a linear ramp: over ten
rows linear gives the top 18%, which nobody experiences as "this is what I want
to work on". Allocation is largest-remainder so the budget is spent exactly, and
what a exhausted bucket cannot take flows down the list rather than shrinking the
session -- otherwise a plan would quietly become a cap.

A plan cannot excuse you from review. It decides which *new* material is woven in
and at what share; every owed card is still owed, in the same order.

`policies/` finally gets the `get()`/`names()` registry that `srs/`, `graders/`
and `presenters/` have had all along, plus the `SessionPolicy` protocol
`ARCHITECTURE.md` has listed as an extension point since the beginning.

## Issues

`material_issues` is deliberately not `card_reports`. That table says one
exercise is broken and suspends the card; this says the grouping is wrong and
suspends nothing. Same reasoning that keeps reports out of `review_log`.

## The tab

Drag-to-reorder priorities, three knobs, and a live preview of what tomorrow
would look like. The preview is cheap because the policy is pure, which is what
makes a knob an experiment rather than a commitment.

ADR-0005 governs the new endpoints and is easy to break by accident: card ids are
authored from the material, so a quarter of them are the answer. The catalogue
returns counts and labels only -- never a card id, never a note id, never a note
field -- and a test asserts that over raw response bytes rather than a parsed
field, because a parsed assertion only checks the places you thought to look.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

* fix(store): never stamp a database's schema version backwards

An older build opening a newer database wrote its own `SCHEMA_VERSION` over the
recorded one. The next time the newer build ran, the version it read was lower
than the migration it had already applied, so it replayed it -- "duplicate column
name" on a database that was fine until something read it.

Not theoretical here. The hub serves repetita live from the working tree, so
switching branches over one study database is an ordinary thing to do, and this
change adds the first migration anyone would hit it with.

The stamp now takes the greater of the two.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(content): read a course's tags as facets (#50)
entry.content:
feat(content): read a course's tags as facets (#50)

`notes.tags` is a JSON array in a TEXT column. It has been written by every sync
since the beginning and read by no query at all, because a JSON blob cannot be
indexed, joined or grouped. Measured across the real course: 676 notes whose
tags mix four different kinds of statement in one namespace -- level (A1/A2/B1),
track (vocabulario/gramatica/musica/fala), topic (tempo/comida/preposicoes) and
provenance (licao-setembro) -- with nothing in the engine able to tell them
apart.

So "the A2 grammar cards about prepositions that are still new" could not be
expressed, let alone counted.

A per-course `facets.yaml` says which question each tag answers, and
`note_facets` is the join table that makes GROUP BY possible.

The tags themselves do not change, and that is deliberate. `importers/hub.py`
records that the predecessor had `track`, `topic` and `level` as three separate
columns and the import flattened them into tags on purpose, because "a tag is
the general form of something true about this note that a course may weight or
filter on". An axis is a reading of that bag, not a replacement for it. No note
file is rewritten by this change.

A note may hold several values on one axis. That is the ordinary case rather
than an edge one: material about ordering food in a market is genuinely both
`comida` and `cidade`, and forcing a choice loses real information. Only `level`
is capped, at one, because two levels would make every count by level disagree
with the total.

One axis may be `catch_all`, which is what makes adding a topic an edit to a
note rather than to a course's configuration. Declared values beat the
catch-all, so promoting a value onto a real axis reclassifies it everywhere with
no note touched.

Taxonomy problems are never fatal. A note filed under nothing is badly filed,
not broken, and quarantining it would take working material away from a learner
over a bookkeeping mistake -- the opposite of what the quarantine is for.

Classification reads the stored notes rather than the incoming files, which
matters under ADR-0006: a note edited here keeps its own tags, and filing the
file's version would put it under something it no longer says.

`facets.yaml` is optional. A course without one gets no axes and no complaints,
so every course written before this is still valid.

`docs/tagging.md` documents the conventions and the loop for changing tags,
written to be actionable by an agent working from an issue -- including the part
that is easy to get wrong in both directions: renaming a tag is safe, because
nothing is keyed on it, unlike an item id.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(content): load unit.yaml and the course path (#49)
entry.content:
feat(content): load unit.yaml and the course path (#49)

Three pieces of authored structure reached no query at all.

`unit.yaml` was skipped outright by the loader -- `if path.name == "unit.yaml":
continue` -- so a unit's title and CEFR level were written by the author, sat in
the course directory, and were read by nothing. `Course.path` declares the order
units are meant to be taken in and the prerequisites between them; it was parsed
into a typed model and never looked at. `Course.tag_weights` is documented as
"relative share of each tag when new material is introduced" and had no reader
either.

So: a `Unit` model, a `units` table and a `courses` table, populated by the same
merge that owns the rest of the material.

Ordering comes from `path` where a course declares one. A unit the path does not
mention sorts *after* every unit it does, in directory order, rather than at the
front -- an unlisted unit is material the author has not placed yet, and it
should not jump the sequence they did place.

A missing `unit.yaml` is not a problem. A unit exists because its directory
does; the file only decorates it, and its absence means a unit with no title
yet, which is the normal state of a course being written.

Units are archived rather than deleted, for the same reason notes are:
`notes.unit` joins on this id, and a unit that leaves the files still names the
unit its notes were studied under.

No migration and no version bump. `courses` and `units` are wholly new tables,
and `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` in `SCHEMA` reaches an existing database on the
next connect -- which is exactly the case the contract beside `MIGRATIONS` says
needs no step.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>

entry.title: feat(store): the database owns the material (#48)
entry.content:
feat(store): the database owns the material (#48)

ADR-0006. `courses/*.yaml` becomes an import/export format; `notes` and `cards`
stop being a cache that is wiped and re-derived on every load.

`sync()` merges instead of replacing. Four outcomes per note: inserted when it
is new, left alone when the source is unchanged, updated when the source
changed, and -- the one the design turns on -- a reported *conflict* when a note
was edited here and changed at the source. The local note stays and the id comes
back in the report. Choosing a winner automatically is the only behaviour that
would make an import unsafe to run, because the loser is unrecoverable and
nothing in the UI would say so.

A note that has left the files is archived, never deleted. Deleting would orphan
`card_state` rows whose history cannot be reconstructed from anything. That is
also why this schema still has no foreign keys: ownership makes the old
reasoning stronger, not weaker, since a note removed in the app must never
cascade into someone's schedule.

The property that used to be free is now maintained on purpose. "A card whose
note vanishes keeps its history" held because nothing linked the tables -- a
property of the *absence* of a mechanism. Archiving replaces that absence with a
mechanism, so the guarantee is re-pinned rather than inherited: a removed note's
row survives, its `card_state` survives, material that comes back returns on the
schedule it left with, and no sequence of imports changes `review_log`.

Archived rows must be excluded by every content query or archived material stays
in circulation. Two needed it: the session queue and `card_ids()`.
`lesson_first_seen_on` deliberately does not -- it counts answers that really
were given, and an answer is not retracted by its note leaving the course.

`content_hash` covers the note as authored and excludes `origin`: moving a note
to another file is not a change to the material, and hashing the path would turn
any reorganisation of a course into a wall of conflicts.

`sync()` now returns a `SyncReport` rather than a bare pair of counts. A merge
that cannot report a conflict is a merge that hides one.

Export is owed next. The README promises that adding a lesson is a pull request
a non-programmer can make, and once material can be edited here that promise
depends on writing it back out.

Signed-off-by: Michał Weiss <mikub97@gmail.com>
